steps.say: Filling studies separate bladder pressure from tummy pressure. Detrusor pressure is worked out by subtracting the rectal balloon reading from the total bladder reading. Without this step a cough looks like a bladder squeeze, so the diagnosis is always read from the detrusor line alone.
steps.tx: **Pdet** (detrusor pressure) during **filling cystometry** (bladder pressure study) is calculated continuously by subtracting intra-abdominal pressure (**Pabd**, via rectal balloon) from total intravesical pressure (**Pves**, bladder catheter reading). Without subtraction a cough or strain mimics a contraction, so every modern trace displays all three lines and diagnosis is read from Pdet alone.

rows: Total intravesical pressure from bladder catheter
Pves minus Pabd, the true detrusor pressure
Coughs read from Pdet, never from Pves alone

steps.say: Compliance describes how quietly the bladder stores urine. It is the change in volume divided by the change in detrusor pressure. Values under twelve to twenty millilitres per centimetre of water identify a dangerously stiff bladder that passes storage pressure straight to the kidneys.
steps.tx: Normal **bladder compliance** (storage distensibility) equals volume change over detrusor pressure change (**Delta-V**/**Delta-Pdet** ratio), with values below **12 to 20 mL/cmH2O** (twelve to twenty millilitres per centimetre of water) indicating dangerously low compliance. A stiff bladder transmits storage pressure to the upper tracts, so compliance decides whether the kidneys stay safe during filling.

rows: Whether kidneys stay safe in filling

steps.say: Leak point pressure predicts kidney damage. A detrusor leak point above forty centimetres of water in neurogenic patients strongly predicts deterioration of the upper tracts with swelling and scarring. Lasting storage pressure overwhelms the ureters, so crossing forty commits the patient to pressure lowering treatment.
steps.tx: **Detrusor leak point pressure** (**DLPP**, pressure at which leakage starts) exceeding **40 cmH2O** (forty centimetres of water) in neurogenic patients strongly predicts **upper tract damage** (upper urinary tract deterioration) with hydronephrosis and secondary renal injury. Sustained storage pressure overwhelms ureteral peristalsis and refluxes urine upward, so passing 40 obliges pressure-lowering management.

vis.alt: Diagram of urinary tract obstruction sites with upstream hydronephrosis.
vis.caption: Sustained pressure produces hydronephrosis of the type DLPP above 40 predicts. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Lesions above the pons send excess signals down an intact cord. Stroke and Parkinson disease typically produce bladder overactivity with coordinated sphincter relaxation, so voiding stays normal in pattern. The bladder contracts too often but empties cleanly, and treatment remains aimed at urgency rather than catheters.
steps.tx: **Suprapontine lesion** (brain lesion above the pons) from stroke or Parkinson disease usually cause **detrusor overactivity** (involuntary bladder contractions) with coordinated sphincter relaxation, keeping voiding synergy normal. The bladder contracts too often but empties cleanly, so voiding remains clean and treatment targets urgency and frequency with antimuscarinics or beta-3 agonists instead of catheters.

rows: Antimuscarinics or beta-3 agonists, not catheters

steps.say: Lesions between the pons and sacrum remove coordination. Neck and chest cord injuries above T6 cause the bladder and the sphincter to squeeze at the same time. The bladder pushes against a shut outlet, pressures turn dangerous, and emptying stays poor.
steps.tx: **Suprasacral cord injury** (spinal lesion between pons and sacrum), including cervical and thoracic trauma above **T6** (sixth thoracic level), causes **detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia** (**DSD**, bladder contracting against a closed sphincter): involuntary detrusor contraction coincides with involuntary external urethral sphincter closure. Squeezing against a shut outlet generates dangerous pressures with poor emptying, threatening continence and the upper tracts.

rows: Involuntary closure at the same time

steps.say: High cord injuries come with a cardiovascular emergency. Overstretching of a full bladder in lesions at or above T6 triggers sudden life threatening high blood pressure with pounding headache, slow pulse, and sweating above the injury. Rapid bladder drainage aborts most attacks, and every such patient needs a written emergency plan.
steps.tx: **Autonomic dysreflexia** (sympathetic storm from cord injury) occurs with a **T6 cord lesion** (spinal injury at or above T6) or higher, where bladder overdistension triggers **paroxysmal hypertension** (sudden life-threatening blood pressure surge) with severe headache, slow pulse, and sweating above the injury line. Immediate bladder drainage aborts most episodes, and every patient carries a plan for rapid recognition, sitting upright, and emptying the bladder.

rows: T6 or above, sympathetic storm zone
Surging pressure, headache, slow pulse, sweating
Sit upright, drain bladder at once

steps.say: Sacral injuries leave the bladder silent. Damage to the conus, the cauda equina, or the pelvic nerves during pelvic surgery leaves a bladder that neither squeezes nor holds pressure safely. Retention with overflow leakage becomes the rule, and the upper tracts need scheduled imaging.
steps.tx: Sacral and infrasacral lesions of the **conus medullaris** (cord tip) and **cauda equina** (lumbar-sacral root bundle), or pelvic plexus surgery, produce an **acontractile detrusor** (bladder that cannot contract) with low compliance and no voluntary sphincter control. Retention with overflow incontinence becomes the rule, and the upper tracts need scheduled surveillance imaging.

rows: Conus medullaris, cauda equina, pelvic plexus
Retention with overflow, image upper tracts

steps.say: Emptying failure is managed with a catheter the patient passes. Intermittent self catheterization several times daily, introduced by Lapides, remains the gold standard for incomplete emptying and nerve related retention. It keeps pressures low and protects the kidneys better than any permanent tube.
steps.tx: **Clean intermittent catheterization** (**CIC**, self-passed sterile catheter), introduced by **Lapides** (pioneering urologist), stays the cornerstone gold standard for incomplete emptying and nerve-related retention. Used several times daily alongside fluid discipline, it holds pressures down, empties residual urine, and guards the kidneys better than any permanent tube, with antimuscarinics added when overactivity continues between passes.
